slides: Okay, before the advanced practice, here's a quick summary of the harder questions.
Three things make them harder. A crowded figure, letters, and a missing line.
Several pairs of lines? Take one pair and its transversal. Ignore the rest.
Move the angle you know to the place you need. Then go to the next pair.
Then build the equation.
Here's a quick shortcut. Six plus eight is fourteen, so x has to end in six. Only forty-six does.
Lost? Look for an anchor. Angles that make a straight line, or a full circle.
Every angle gives you its neighbor. A hundred eighty minus it.
Letters instead of numbers? Put numbers back. Looks obtuse? Plug in a hundred thirty.
Then plug the same numbers into the choices. Cross out every choice that doesn't give thirty.
And check that the four choices come out different. If two of them tie, plug in again.
Angles that overlap count a piece twice.
m, n and k cover the full turn, and x one more time. So x is their sum minus three hundred sixty.
No straight transversal? Add an auxiliary line. Through the bend, parallel to both lines.
It splits x into two pieces. And each piece makes a Z with a given angle.
Well, the hard part is seeing that you need a line at all.
Now, the shortcut. Look where each angle's tip points.
Two bends? Same rule. Left side equals right side.
Not sure? A parallel line through each bend always works.
So, before you start, always ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: adding only one side of the zig-zag, and forgetting that overlapping angles count a piece twice.
Okay, now it's your turn. Good luck.
